analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for former members of Congress to ever lobby again.
analysis.headline: A bill to permanently ban former members of Congress from lobbying died without a committee vote after being referred to the House Judiciary Committee in April 2024.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal criminal law so that any former senator or representative who makes a lobbying contact with executive branch officials or current members of Congress would face criminal penalties [S2]. Unlike the current one-to-two-year 'cooling off' rules, this would be a lifetime ban for former members, with criminal punishment under the same provisions used for other federal lobbying crimes [S2]. It would also impose a one-year ban on former elected officers of the House, such as the Clerk or Sergeant at Arms, from lobbying the House [S2]. The bill was introduced at the end of April 2024 and never moved past its committee referral before the term ended [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who want lawmakers to stop converting their time in office into high-paying lobbying careers. The bill's sponsor, Rep. Jared Golden of Maine, framed it as a check on the revolving door between Congress and K Street [S1].

how_it_helps.text: It would make any lobbying contact by a former member of Congress a criminal offense, punishable under the same statute as other federal lobbying crimes, rather than the current civil cooling-off rules [S2].
The ban would last for life, with no waiting period, closing the path by which departing lawmakers commonly take jobs influencing their former colleagues [S2].
It would also bar former elected House officers from lobbying the House for one year after leaving [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress and the lobbying industry built around them, who would lose access to one of the most valuable forms of insider influence available. Lobbying firms would lose the ability to hire recently departed lawmakers as rainmakers.

drawbacks.text: A lifetime ban is broader than any current federal rule and would face constitutional challenges on free speech and petition grounds, since the Supreme Court has never upheld a total lifetime restriction on former officials lobbying [S2].

The bill would not touch executive branch lobbying by former executive officials, and it does not address the many other channels of influence, such as campaign fundraising and 'strategic advisor' roles that do not involve formal lobbying contacts [S2].
Critics of broad revolvers sometimes argue that harsh bans can push influence work into unregistered 'shadow lobbying' that is harder to police, which this bill does not address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A lifetime criminal ban would be the strongest revolving-door restriction ever enacted for members of Congress, and its main cost falls on the lobbying economy rather than on working people. The real weakness is not the cost but the design: it does nothing about the informal, unregistered influence work that would simply continue, and it may not survive a court challenge. Still, as a statement of where the law should draw the line, it is a genuinely meaningful proposal.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a markup, a hearing, or a floor vote before the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Golden of Maine introduced the bill on April 30, 2024, as Congress approached its summer work period [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S4].
The committee took no further action, and no vote was ever scheduled, leaving the bill to die at the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025 [S4].
Only one other House member cosponsored the bill, giving it the bare minimum of support needed to stay alive on paper but not to move it [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress and the lobbying firms that hire them, who keep unrestricted access to their former colleagues now that the bill died without a vote.

for.name: Jared Golden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a markup, hearing, or vote after its April 2024 referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred. The bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and no Republicans publicly supported or opposed it in the record.

industries.note: The bill would remove the single most valuable hire in the industry: a former member of Congress with personal relationships in both chambers. Its death preserves that business model unchanged. The industry's interest runs against the public's in this fight, since its revenue depends on selling access that ordinary voters cannot buy.

With the bill dead, departing lawmakers keep their current cooling-off periods and lifetime earning potential in lobbying, where former members routinely command large salaries. Their interest in the status quo is directly opposite to the bill's goal.
